Radzanow Jewish Cemetery

Jewish Cemetery · Radzanów, Poland

Demolished. Radzanów, a 13th-century settlement granted Chełmno rights in 1400, was a noted center of cloth production; Jewish settlement developed in the second half of the 18th century after town owner Dorota Niszczycka donated two streets and cemetery/synagogue land in 1765, granting broad trading privileges - the first arrivals had been expelled from nearby Szereńsk. Population reached 375 by 1827; an 1823-1862 settlement ban for outside Jews (due to the town's border location) didn't prevent the community from nearly doubling, reaching 57% (612) by 1856. Losing town rights in 1869 following the January Uprising, the debt-ridden town was sold to Samuel Konitz, a Polonized Jewish family from Pomerania, whose sons managed it until 1912. By 1921, 303 (23%) endured wartime repression and forced labor before roughly 200 survivors were deported to the Mława Ghetto in November 1941, then to Treblinka and Auschwitz. This cemetery, established following the 1765 privilege, was enclosed with an earth rampart and fence by 1775, with a two-room caretaker's and funeral house on the grounds. Germans destroyed the site in spring 1940, repurposing tombstones and the fence; synagogue books were burned there as well. Postwar, part of the grounds (where the funeral house stood) was sold to a private farm owner under Communist rule.
